source_text: Ἔοικεν δὲ ὁ παιδαγωγὸς ἡμῶν, ὦ παῖδες ὑμεῖς,· τῷ πατρὶ τῷ αὑτοῦ τῷ θεῷ, οὗπέρ ἐστιν υἱός, ἀναμάρτητος, ἀνεπίληπτος καὶ ἀπαθὴς τὴν ψυχήν, θεὸς ἐν ἀνθρώπου σχήματι ἄχραντος, πατρικῷ θελήματι διάκονος, λόγος θεός, ὁ ἐν τῷ πατρί, ὁ ἐκ δεξιῶν τοῦ πατρός, σὺν καὶ τῷ σχήματι θεός· οὗτος ἡμῖν εἰκὼν ἡ ἀκηλίδωτος, τούτῳ παντὶ σθένει πειρατέον ἐξομοιοῦν τὴν ψυχήν· ἀλλ᾿ ὃ μὲν ἀπόλυτος εἰς τὸ παντελὲς ἀνθρωπίνων παθῶν, διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ μόνος κριτής, ὅτι ἀναμάρτητος μόνος· ἡμεῖς δέ, ὅση δύναμις, ὡς ὅτι ἐλάχιστα ἁμαρτάνειν πειρώμεθα. κατεπείγει γὰρ οὐδὲν τοσοῦτον ὡς ἡ τῶν παθῶν καὶ νοσημάτων ἀπαλλαγὴ πρῶτον, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ ἡ κώλυσις τῆς εἰς τὴν συνήθειαν τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων εὐεμπτωσίας. ἄριστον μὲν οὖν τὸ μηδ᾿ ὅλως ἐξαμαρτάνειν κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον, ὃ δή φαμεν εἶναι θεοῦ· δεύτερον δὲ τὸ μηδενὸς τῶν κατὰ γνώμην ἐφάψασθαί ποτε ἀδικημάτων, ὅπερ οἰκεῖον σοφοῦ· τρίτον δὲ τὸ μὴ πάνυ πολλοῖς τῶν ἀκουσίων περιπεσεῖν, ὅπερ ἴδιον παιδαγωγουμένων εὐγενῶς· τὸ δὲ μὴ ἐπὶ μήκιστον διατρῖψαι τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασι τελευταῖον τετάχθω· ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦτο [δὲ] τοῖς εἰς μετάνοιαν ἀνακαλουμένοις ἀναμαχέσασθαι σωτήριον. καί μοι δοκεῖ παγκάλως διὰ Μωσέως φάσκειν ὁ παιδαγωγός »ἐάν τις ἀποθάνῃ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ αἰφνίδιον, παραχρῆμα μιανθήσεται ἡ κεφαλὴ εὐχῆς αὐτοῦ καὶ ξυρήσεται«, τὴν ἀκούσιον ἁμαρτίαν αἰφνίδιον θάνατον προσειπών· μιαίνειν δὲ αὐτὸν λέγει κηλιδοῦντα τὴν ψυχήν· διὸ καὶ τὴν θεραπείαν ᾗ τάχος ὑποτίθεται ξυρᾶσθαι παραχρῆμα τὴν κεφαλὴν συμβουλεύων, τὰς ἑπισκιαζούσας τῷ λογισμῷ τῆς ἀγνοίας κόμας ἀποψήξασθαι παραινῶν, ὡς γυμνὸν δασείας καταλειφθέντα ὕλης (τῆς κακίας) τὸν λογισμὸν (ἐνθρονίζεται δὲ οὗτος ἐν ἐγκεφάλῳ) ἐπὶ τὴν μετάνοιαν παλινδρομῆσαι. ἔπειτα ὀλίγα προσειπὼν ἐπιφέρει »αἱ δὲ ἡμέραι αἱ πρότεραι ἄλογοι«, δι᾿ ὧν δῆλον ὅτι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι μηνύονται αἱ μὴ γεγονυῖαι κατὰ λόγον. καὶ τὸ μὲν ἀκούσιον αἰφνίδιον προσεῖπεν, τὸ δὲ ἁμαρτάνειν ἄλογον. οὗ δὴ χάριν ὁ λόγος ὁ παιδαγωγὸς τὴν ἐπιστασίαν εἴληχεν εἰς τὴν ἀλόγου κώλυσιν ἁμαρτίας. σκόπει δὲ ἐνθένδε ἀπὸ τῆς γραφῆς »διὰ τοῦτο τάδε λέγει κύριος«· τὸ ἁμάρτημα ἐλεγκτικῶς τὸ προυπάρξαν διὰ τῆς ἑπομένης δείκνυται ῥήσεως, καθὸ ἡ δικαία κρίσις ἕπεται, καὶ τοῦτο ἐμφανῶς διὰ τῶν προφητῶν καταφαίνεται, ὡς, εἰ μὴ ἥμαρτες, λεγόντων, οὐκ ἂν τάδε ἠπείλησεν, καὶ »διὰ τοῦτο οὕτως λέγει κύριος« καὶ »ἀνθ᾿ ὧν οὐκ ἠκούσατε τῶν λόγων τούτων, διὰ τοῦτο τάδε λέγει κύριος« καὶ »διὰ τοῦτο ἰδοὺ λέγει κύριος«. διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ ἡ προφητεία, δι᾿ ὑπακοὴν καὶ παρακοήν, δι᾿ ἣν μὲν ἵνα σωθῶμεν, δι᾿ ἣν δὲ ἵνα παιδευθῶμεν. Ἔστιν οὖν ὁ παιδαγωγὸς ἡμῶν λόγος διὰ παραινέσεων θεραπευτικὸς τῶν παρὰ φύσιν τῆς ψυχῆς παθῶν. κυρίως μὲν γὰρ ἡ τῶν τοῦ σώματος νοσημάτων βοήθεια ἰατρικὴ καλεῖται, τέχνη ἀνθρωπίνῃ σοφίᾳ διδακτή. λόγος δὲ ὁ πατρικὸς μόνος ἐστὶν ἀνθρωπίνων ἰατρὸς ἀρρωστημάτων παιώνιος καὶ ἐπῳδὸς ἅγιος νοσούσης ψυχῆς. »σῶσον τὸν δοῦλόν σου,« φησίν, »ὁ θεός μου, τὸν ἐλπίζοντα ἐπὶ σοί· ἐλέησόν με, κύριε, ὅτι πρὸς σὲ κεκράξομαι ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν.« »ἰατρικὴ μὲν γὰρ« κατὰ Δημόκριτον »σώματος νόσους ἀκέεται, σοφίη δὲ ψυχὴν παθῶν ἀφαιρεῖται«· ὁ δὲ ἀγαθὸς παιδαγωγός, ἡ σοφία, ὁ λόγος τοῦ πατρός, ὁ δημιουργήσας τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ὅλου κήδεται τοῦ πλάσματος, καὶ σῶμα καὶ ψυχὴν ἀκεῖται αὐτοῦ ὁ πανακὴς τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος ἰατρός. ὁ σωτὴρ »ἀνάστα,« φησὶ τῷ παρειμένῳ, »τὸν σκίμποδα ἐφ᾿ ὃν κατάκεισαι λαβὼν ἄπιθι οἴκαδε«. παραχρῆμα δὲ ὁ ἄρρωστος ἐρρώσθη. καὶ τῷ τεθνεῶτι »Λάζαρε,« εἶπεν, »ἔξιθι«· ὃ δὲ ἐξῆλθεν τῆς σοροῦ, ὁ νεκρός, οἷος ἦν πρὶν ἢ παθεῖν, μελετήσας τὴν ἀνάστασιν. ναὶ μὴν καὶ καθ᾿ αὑτὴν ἰᾶται τὴν ψυχὴν ἐντολαῖς καὶ χαρίσμασιν, ἀλλὰ ταῖς μὲν ὑποθήκαις τάχα δὴ μέλλει· χαρίσμασι δὲ πλούσιος »ἀφέωνται σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι« τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς ἡμῖν λέγει. ἡμεῖς δὲ ἅμα νοήματι νήπιοι γεγόναμεν, τὴν ἀρίστην καὶ βεβαιοτάτην τάξιν παρὰ τῆς αὐτοῦ εὐταξίας μεταλαμβάνοντες, ἣ πρῶτον μὲν ἀμφὶ τὸν κόσμον καὶ τὸν οὐρανὸν τάς τε ἡλιακὰς περιδινήσεις κύκλους τε καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἄστρων τὰς φορὰς ἀσχολεῖται διὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ἔπειτα δὲ περὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον αὐτόν, περὶ ὃν ἡ πᾶσα σπουδὴ καταγίνεται· καὶ τοῦτον ἔργον ἡγουμένη μέγιστον, ψυχὴν μὲν αὐτοῦ φρονήσει καὶ σωφροσύνῃ κατηύθυνεν, τὸ δὲ σῶμα κάλλει καὶ εὐρυθμίᾳ συνεκεράσατο, περὶ δὲ τὰς πράξεις τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος τό τε ἐν αὐταῖς κατορθοῦν καὶ τὸ εὔτακτον ἐνέπνευσεν τὸ αὐτῆς.
thought_title: Our Instructor's Treatment of Our Sins
pass_a_gloss: But our Instructor seems to be like the Father, God, whose Son He is, sinless, blameless, and passionless in soul, God in human form, unblemished, a servant by the Father's will, the Word of God, who is in the Father, who is at the Father's right hand, and is God even in human form; this One is our unchanging image, and we must try to make our soul like Him in every way; but He is completely free from human passions, and for this reason He is the only Judge, because He alone is sinless; we, however, try as much as we can to sin as little as possible. For nothing is so urgent as to be freed from passions and diseases first, and then to be prevented from easily falling into the habit of sinning. The best thing, then, is not to sin at all, which we say is a characteristic of God; second is to have never touched any intentional wrongs, which is proper to a wise person; third is not to have fallen into many unintentional sins, which is characteristic of those being instructed nobly; and the last is not to have lingered long in sin; but even this is a struggle that brings salvation to those being called to repentance. And it seems to me that our Instructor says through Moses, 'If anyone dies suddenly, his head will be shaved immediately,' calling sudden death an unintentional sin; and He says that this defiles him, staining his soul; therefore, the treatment He proposes is to shave the head immediately, advising us to cut off the locks of ignorance that overshadow our mind, so that our mind, freed from the material of evil, may return to repentance. Then, adding a few words, He says, 'The former days were unreasoning,' by which it is clear that sins that were not done according to reason are indicated. And He called the unintentional sin 'sudden,' but sinning 'unreasoning.' Therefore, the Word, our Instructor, has taken care to prevent irrational sin. Consider, then, from this Scripture, 'The Lord says this'; the sin that was committed beforehand is shown to be convicted through the following statement, as the just judgment follows, and this is clearly revealed through the prophets, as if they were saying, 'If you had not sinned, He would not have threatened you,' and 'The Lord says this' and 'Because you did not listen to these words, the Lord says this' and 'Therefore the Lord says this.' For prophecy is given for obedience and disobedience, for the sake of which we are either saved or instructed. Our Instructor, then, is the Word, who heals the soul's unnatural passions through exhortations. For the help for bodily diseases is called medical, a human art taught by wisdom. But the paternal Word is the only doctor for human weaknesses, a holy and gentle healer of the sick soul. 'Save your servant,' it says, 'my God, who hopes in you; have mercy on me, Lord, for I cry out to you all day.' 'For medicine,' according to Democritus, 'heals the body's diseases, but wisdom removes the soul's passions.' And the good Instructor, wisdom, the Word of the Father, who created humanity, takes care of the whole creation, and heals both body and soul, the all-sufficient doctor of humanity. The Savior says to the paralytic, 'Get up, take the mat you are lying on, and go home.' And immediately the sick man was healed. And to the dead man, He said, 'Lazarus, come out,' and he came out of the tomb, the dead man, just as he was before he suffered, having practiced resurrection. Yes, and He heals the soul itself with commands and gifts, but perhaps He will do this through proposals; and with gifts, He says to us sinners, 'Your sins will be forgiven.' But we have become foolish in our thinking, receiving the best and most secure order from His own well-orderedness, which first concerns the world and the heaven and the sun's cycles and the orbits of the other stars, all for the sake of humanity; then it concerns humanity itself, about whom all care is taken; and it considers this work to be the greatest, guiding the human soul with prudence and self-control, and shaping the body with beauty and harmony, and inspiring in human actions both what is right and what is well-ordered.

pass_b_english: Our Instructor, children, is like His Father God — the sinless, blameless, passionless Son who is God in human form, unblemished, a servant by the Father's will, the Word of God who dwells in the Father and sits at His right hand, God even in human flesh. This One is our unchanging image, and we must strive with all our strength to make our souls like Him. He is utterly free of human passions; therefore He alone is Judge, because He alone is sinless. We, on the other hand, try as best we can to sin as little as possible. Nothing is so urgent as first being freed from passions and diseases, and then being kept from easily slipping into the habit of sin. The best is not to sin at all in any way — a characteristic we attribute to God. Second is never to have committed any intentional wrong — the mark of a wise person. Third is not to fall into many unintentional sins — the mark of those nobly instructed. Last is not to linger long in sin; yet even this struggle brings salvation to those called to repentance. It seems to me our Instructor speaks beautifully through Moses: "If anyone dies suddenly beside him, the head of his consecration shall be defiled and he shall shave it" (Numbers 6:9), calling sudden death an unintentional sin. He says it defiles him, staining the soul; therefore He prescribes the treatment of shaving the head immediately, urging us to shear off the locks of ignorance that overshadow our reasoning, so that our mind — stripped of the hairy stuff of evil (for the mind sits enthroned in the brain) — may turn back to repentance. Then, adding a few words, He says, "The former days were unreasoning" (Numbers 6:12), making clear that sins not done according to reason are indicated. He called the unintentional sin "sudden," but sinning itself "unreasoning." For this reason the Word our Instructor has taken charge to prevent irrational sin. Consider then from Scripture: "Therefore the Lord says these things." The earlier sin is shown convicted by the following statement, because just judgment follows, and this is plainly revealed through the prophets, as if they were saying, "If you had not sinned, He would not have threatened you," and "Therefore the Lord says this," and "Because you did not listen to these words, the Lord says this," and "Therefore, behold, the Lord says this." For prophecy exists for obedience and disobedience — for the one that we may be saved, for the other that we may be instructed. Our Instructor, then, is the Word who heals the soul's unnatural passions through exhortations. Properly speaking, help for the body's diseases is called medicine, a human art taught by wisdom. But the paternal Word is the only physician for human weaknesses, a holy and gentle healer of the sick soul. "Save Your servant," it says, "my God, the one who hopes in You; have mercy on me, Lord, for I cry to You all day" (Psalm 119:145-152). "For medicine," according to Democritus, "heals the body's diseases, but wisdom removes the soul's passions." And the good Instructor, Wisdom, the Word of the Father who created humanity, cares for the whole creature and heals both body and soul — the all-sufficient doctor of humanity. The Savior says to the paralytic, "Rise, take up your mat and go home" (Matthew 9:6), and immediately the sick man was healed. And to the dead man He said, "Lazarus, come out" (John 11:43); he came out of the tomb, the dead man, just as he was before he suffered, having practiced resurrection. Yes, and He heals the soul itself with commands and gifts — though perhaps He will do so through proposals; yet with gifts He is rich, saying to us sinners, "Your sins are forgiven." But we have become foolish in our thinking, receiving the best and most secure order from His own well-orderedness, which first concerns the world and heaven — the sun's cycles, the circles and courses of the other stars — all for humanity's sake; then it concerns humanity itself, about whom all care is taken. It regards this work as the greatest: guiding the human soul with prudence and self-control, shaping the body with beauty and harmony, and inspiring in human actions both what is right and what is well-ordered.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions of the Greek text, including the nuances of the Instructor's nature (sinless, passionless, etc.) and the distinction between intentional and unintentional sins. Pass A preserves all clauses, and Pass B provides accurate scripture identifications (Numbers 6:9, Psalm 119:145-152, Matthew 9:6, John 11:43) which were alluded to in the Greek. The parenthetical note in the Greek regarding the mind being enthroned in the brain is correctly handled in Pass B. The title 'Our Instructor's Treatment of Our Sins' correctly names the thought of the chapter.
